rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He construes “when you were unjust” as the time when their injustice became clear and undeniable.
rows.anchor: وحمل إذ ظلمتم على معنى إذ تبين ووضح ظلمكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The substitution analysis fails if إذ retains its usual meaning as an adverb of past time; it works only if إذ means an unrestricted time.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز فيه البدل على بقاء إذ على موضوعها من كونها ظرفا لما مضى من الزمان

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes the substitution analysis from Ibn Jinni, who said the afterlife and worldly life are united in God's judgment and knowledge.
rows.anchor: تخريجها على البدل، أخذه الزمخشري من ابن جني

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Ibn Jinni's final explanation treats the two lives as alike in God's knowledge, so إذ can replace “today” as though either were past or future.
rows.anchor: أن الدنيا والآخرة متصلتان، وهما سواء في حكم الله وعلمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One alternative supplies the omitted word “after”: after you were unjust.
rows.anchor: وقيل: التقدير بعد إذ ظلمتم، فحذف المضاف للعلم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another alternative makes إذ a causal particle meaning “since” or “because.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: إذ للتعليل حرفا بمعنى إن

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Hufi attaches “today” to “benefit you” and rejects attaching إذ to it because the two time adverbials differ in meaning.
rows.anchor: قال الحوفي: اليوم ظرف متعلق بينفعكم، ولا يجوز تعلق إذ به

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Hufi instead attaches إذ to the implied sense that their gathering will not benefit them.
rows.anchor: ولكن تكون إذ متعلقة بما دل عليه المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take the subject of “benefit” to be “sharing”; others supply an omitted subject such as their wrongdoing or denial, which governs إذ.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الفاعل محذوف تقديره ظلمكم، أو جحدكم، وهو العامل في إذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh heard the warning but grew more defiant, while God consoled the Prophet with a question: he cannot make the deaf hear or guide the blind.
rows.anchor: وكانت قريش تسمع ذلك، فلا تزداد إلا عتوا واعتراضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three descriptions mean Quraysh's senses cannot help them escape God's punishment; they are deaf, blind, and lost.
rows.anchor: جعلوا صما عميا حيارى، ويريد بهم قريشا، فهم جامعو الأوصاف الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun “them” in the threat of vengeance refers to Quraysh, whose only earlier mention was in the phrase about hearing the deaf.
rows.anchor: ولذلك عاد الضمير عليهم في قوله: فإما نذهبن بك فإنا منهم منتقمون

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority says that if the Prophet dies before victory, God will punish Quraysh in the afterlife; if he sees their promised punishment, such as Badr, God has power over them.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول الجمهور

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan and Qatada say the threatened people are the Prophet's community; God spared him the vengeance other prophets saw in their lifetimes, and punishment came after his death.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وقتادة: المتوعد هم الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading نرينك uses a light nūn.
rows.anchor: وقرىء: نرينك بالنون الخفيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After presenting the alternatives of the Prophet's death or seeing the punishment, God commands him to hold firmly to the revelation.
rows.anchor: أمره بأن يستمسك بما أوحاه إليه

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority reads أوحي in the passive voice.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: أوحي مبنيا للمفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority reads أوحي as passive, while some Syrian readers have a variant reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: أوحي مبنيا للمفعول، وبعض قراء الشام:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation is an honor for the Prophet and his people because it came among them and in their language, making them its recipients.
rows.anchor: أي شرف، حيث نزل عليهم وبلسانهم، جعل تبعا لهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd identify the people as Quraysh and then the Arabs.
rows.anchor: القوم على هذا قريش ثم العرب، قاله ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة والسدي وابن زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet presented himself to tribes and stayed silent when asked who would rule after him until this verse came; then he answered, “Quraysh.”
rows.anchor: فكان إذا سئل عن ذلك قال: «لقريش»

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan takes “your people” to mean the Prophet's community and the remembrance as an admonition.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: القوم هنا أمته، والمعنى: وإنه لتذكرة وموعظة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse shows that people may desire honorable praise; God would not have bestowed remembrance on the Prophet if it were not desirable.
rows.anchor: قيل: وهذه الآية تدل على أن الإنسان يرغب في الثناء الحسن الجميل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's prayer for an enduring good name is another example of seeking worthy remembrance.
rows.anchor: واجعل لي لسان صدق في الآخرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Good remembrance rivals or surpasses life: life's effect reaches only the living, while a good name endures everywhere and in every age.
rows.anchor: والذكر الجميل قائم مقام الحياة، بل هو أفضل من الحياة

rows.speaker: ابن دريد
rows.claim: Ibn Duraid's verse supports the value of leaving a good report behind.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن دريد: وإنما المراد حديث بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second poet likewise says that the world's finest qualities are the good reports that remain.
rows.anchor: وقال الآخر: إنما الدنيا محاسنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hulagu illustrated enduring remembrance by saying that Muhammad, dead for over six hundred years, was still named from minarets five times daily.
rows.anchor: هذا الذي له أزيد من ستمائة سنة، قد مات وهو يذكر على المآذن

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says people will be questioned about gratitude for this blessing.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن عن شكر هذه النعمة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says those who denied the revelation will be questioned in rebuke.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: المراد من كذب به يسأل سؤال توبيخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report has Mikael ask Gabriel whether Muhammad asked; Gabriel says Muhammad is too certain and faithful to need to ask.
rows.anchor: وفي الأثر أن ميكال قال لجبريل: هل سأل محمد عن ذلك؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Zuhri, and Ibn Zayd transmit the report that the Prophet did not ask the prophets.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا، والحسن، ومجاهد، وقتادة، والسدي، وعطاء: أراد واسأل أتباع من أرسلنا وحملة شرائعهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report has Mikael ask Gabriel whether Muhammad asked; Gabriel replies that Muhammad is too certain and faithful to need to ask.
rows.anchor: وفي الأثر أن ميكال قال لجبريل: هل سأل محمد عن ذلك؟

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, and Ata take the command to mean asking the messengers' followers and bearers of their laws.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا، والحسن، ومجاهد، وقتادة، والسدي، وعطاء

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says that the followers report what is in the prophets' books, so asking them is effectively asking the prophets.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: هم إنما يخبرونه عن كتب الرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Questioning is figurative for reflection when literal questioning is impossible, as in poets addressing dwellings or asking the earth who made its rivers.
rows.anchor: والسؤال الواقع مجاز عن النظر، حيث لا يصلح لحقيقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question invites examination of earlier religions: no messenger ever brought worship of anything besides God.
rows.anchor: هل جاءت عبادة الأوثان قط في ملة من ملل الأنبياء؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent address is to any listener investigating religions: ask the earlier communities whether their messengers taught worship of other than God; they will say no.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أنه خطاب للسامع الذي يريد أن يفحص عن الديانات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A far-fetched reading takes the command as “ask Me whom I sent before you,” with من as an interrogative and an implied question about whether earlier messengers taught other gods.
rows.anchor: وأبعد من ذهب إلى أن المعنى: واسألني، واسألنا عن من أرسلنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story of Pharaoh follows Quraysh's demand that revelation go to a wealthy notable: Pharaoh also boasted of Egypt's rule, yet Moses overcame him, as will happen to Quraysh.
rows.anchor: اختيارهم أن ينزل القرآن على رجل من القريتين عظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story also follows the command to ask earlier messengers: Moses and Jesus had many followers, and both taught worship of God alone, never other gods.
rows.anchor: ذكر وقته موسى وعيسى، وهما أكبر أتباعا ممن سبقهم من الأنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' signs are the miracles he brought.
rows.anchor: وآيات موسى هي المعجزات التي أتى بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels are singled out as the nobles, whom other people follow.
rows.anchor: وخص الملائكة بالذكر، وهم الأشراف لأن غيرهم من الناس تبع لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before Moses showed the signs, the people had demanded proof that his claim to be God's messenger was true.
rows.anchor: قبله كلام محذوف تقديره: فطالبوه بما يدل على صحة دعواه الرسالة من الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs included the staff turning into a serpent and back, and Moses' hand shining white before returning to its former color.
rows.anchor: وهي انقلاب العصا ثعبانا وعودها عصا، وإخراج اليد البيضاء نيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people laughed immediately, without reflection, in mockery and contempt, just as Quraysh did.
rows.anchor: فاجأهم الضحك بحيث لم يفكروا ولم يتأملوا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies an implicit verb of sudden occurrence to govern إذا after لما, as if the people suddenly entered the time of laughter.
rows.anchor: لأن فعل المفاجأة معها مقدر، وهو عامل النصب في محلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says no grammarian supports that analysis; إذا may instead be a particle, a locative adverb governed by an explicit predicate, or a temporal adverb governed by the predicate.
rows.anchor: ولا نعلم نحويا ذهب إلى ما ذهب إليه هذا الرجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If no predicate follows or a circumstantial noun does, إذا serves as the predicate; a temporal reading with a concrete subject requires an understood omission.
rows.anchor: وإن لم يذكر بعد الاسم خبر، أو ذكر اسم منصوب على الحال، كانت إذا خبرا للمبتدأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The meaning does not show that surprise comes from the preceding clause; it comes from the clause containing إذا.
rows.anchor: بل المعنى يدل على أن المفاجأة تكون من الكلام الذي فيه إذا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains “its sister” as another sign like it, with each sign greater than the rest when compared successively.
rows.anchor: أختها التي هي آية مثلها على سبيل التفضيل والاستقراء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He says the apparent contradiction is resolved because the signs' greatness is nearly equal and observers may rank them differently.
rows.anchor: أنهن موصوفات بالكبر، لا يكدن يتفاوتن فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People can alternate in ranking closely matched things; the Hamasa verse compares such leaders to stars, and al-Anmariyya could not distinguish her sons' nearly equal merits.
rows.anchor: فعلى هذا بنى الناس كلامهم فقالوا: رأيت رجالا بعضهم أفضل من بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan summarizes al-Zamakhshari's account as metaphorical greatness measured relative to the observers.
rows.anchor: ملخصه: أن الوصف بالأكبرية مجاز، وأن ذلك بالنسبة إلى الناظرين فيها

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya reads the wording as describing the signs' increasingly sharp and novel impact on their observers.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: عبارة عن شدة موقعها في نفوسهم بحدة أمرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poet's line supports Ibn Atiyya's point that even old wounds may be forgiven while the latest injury receives attention.
rows.anchor: على إنها تعفو الكلوم وإنما

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says the signs here are proofs and clear evidences.
rows.anchor: وذهب الطبري إلى أن الآيات هنا الحجج والبينات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says every sign was great and each exceeded its predecessor; an omitted “previous” avoids contradiction, and the first sign has no predecessor.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كانت من كبار الآيات، وكانت كل واحدة أكبر من التي قبلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation says the second sign adds knowledge to the first, increasing the strength of the evidence.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الأولى تقتضي علما، والثانية تقتضي علما منضما إلى علم الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling one sign another's “sister” means it resembles or corresponds to it.
rows.anchor: وكنى بأختها: مناسبتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishments included drought, reduced fruit, flood, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood; they were signs meant to turn the people from disbelief.
rows.anchor: بالسنين، ونقص من الثمرات والطوفان والجراد والقمل والضفادع والدم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says God wanted the people to return from disbelief to faith, but without coercion they chose not to return.
rows.anchor: أراد أن يرجعوا عن الكفر إلى الإيمان

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan identifies al-Zamakhshari's account of divine willing as the Mu'tazilite position.
rows.anchor: وهو على طريق الاعتزال

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says لعل expresses expectation according to what humans suppose.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: لعلهم، ترج بحسب معتقد البشر وظنهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The example of rescue to shore shows that people may resume associating partners once saved.
rows.anchor: إذا هم يشركون ، ثم إذا كشفنا عنه ضره مر كأن لم يدعنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison says that relief makes a person act as though he never prayed through distress.
rows.anchor: ثم إذا كشفنا عنه ضره مر كأن لم يدعنا إلى ضر مسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The covenant phrase may mean that Moses prayer is answered.
rows.anchor: وقوله: بما عهد عندك، محتمل أن يكون من أن دعوتك مستجابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax omits Moses prayer and Gods removal of the punishment before “when We removed it.”
rows.anchor: وفي الكلام حذف، أي فدعا موسى، فكشف فلما كشفنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call likely addressed Egypts elite at their meeting place, with Pharaoh raising his voice so his words spread.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه نادى عظماء القبط في محله الذي هو وهم يجتمعون فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Nile channels Pharaoh named included the River of the King, Tulun, Damietta, and Tinnis.
rows.anchor: وأعظمها: نهر الملك، ونهر طولون، ونهر دمياط، ونهر تنيس

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة
rows.claim: Abu Haywa reads ينكثون with a kasra on the kaf.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو حيوة: ينكثون، بكسر الكاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh made his people the audience of the call, apparently addressing Egypt's elite at their meeting place and raising his voice so the message would spread.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه نادى عظماء القبط في محله الذي هو وهم يجتمعون فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call could also be attributed to Pharaoh because he ordered someone to proclaim it.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون أمر بالنداء، فأسند إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh feared the people's allegiance to Moses after seeing God answer Moses' prayer and lift the punishment.
rows.anchor: أنه لما رأى إجابة الله دعوة موسى ورفع العذاب، خاف ميل القوم إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's kingdom of Egypt extended from Alexandria to Aswan.
rows.anchor: وهي من إسكندرية إلى أسوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rivers are interpreted as branches or channels of the Nile.
rows.anchor: وهذه الأنهار: أي الخلجان التي تجري من النيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The waw in “and these rivers” introduces a circumstantial clause; “these rivers” is an adjective or apposition, though coordination with “kingdom” is also possible.
rows.anchor: والواو في وهذه الأنهار واو الحال، وتجري خبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From beneath me” means beneath Pharaoh's control and rule.
rows.anchor: من تحتي: أي من تحت قهري وملكي

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says Pharaoh's gardens and rivers flowed beneath his palace.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: كانت جنانها وأنهارها تجري من تحت قصره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says Pharaoh had a great throne and diverted part of the Nile into channels flowing beneath it.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كان له سرير عظيم، وقطع من نيل مصر قطعة قسمها أنهارا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak interprets the rivers as commanders and powerful chiefs marching under Pharaoh's banner; Abu Hayyan calls this interpretation far-fetched.
rows.anchor: وأبعد الضحاك في تفسيره الأنهار بالقواد والرؤساء الجبابرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret the rivers as wealth, which Pharaoh controlled.
rows.anchor: ومن فسرها بالأموال، يعرفها من تحت يده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret them as horses, since a horse can also be called a river.
rows.anchor: ومن فسرها بالخيل فقيل: كما سمي الفرس بحرا يسمى نهرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says the interpretations of rivers as leaders, wealth, or horses resemble esoteric exegesis.
rows.anchor: وهذه الأقوال الثلاثة تقرب من تفاسير الباطنية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's rhetorical question boasts of his greatness and power while belittling Moses as helpless.
rows.anchor: أفلا تبصرون عظمتي وقدرتي وعجز موسى

rows.speaker: مهدي بن الصفير
rows.claim: Mahdi ibn al-Sufayr reads يبصرون with the third-person yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مهدي بن الصفير: يبصرون، بياء الغيبة

rows.speaker: عيسى
rows.claim: Isa reads أفلا تبصرون with a kasra on the nūn.
rows.anchor: وكسر نون أفلا تبصرون، عيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anecdote: al-Rashid read the verse, promised Egypt to his best servant, and appointed al-Khasib, who was performing ablution.
rows.anchor: وعن الرشيد، أنه لما قرأها قال: لأولينها أحسن عبيدي

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن طاهر
rows.claim: Abdullah ibn Tahir turned back rather than enter Egypt, saying it was too insignificant for him despite being the land Pharaoh had boasted of.
rows.anchor: أهي القرية التي افتخر بها فرعون حتى قال: أليس لي ملك مصر؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent reading takes أم as a disconnected “rather, is it that I am better?”; Pharaoh expects his subjects to affirm that he is the powerful ruler.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أنها أم المنقطعة المقدرة ببل والهمزة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi and Abu Ubayda take أم to mean بل, introducing Pharaoh's claim that he is better than Moses; a poem illustrates this transition.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي وأبو عبيدة: أم بمعنى بل

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh treats أم as a connected alternative: do they see, or do they see that Pharaoh is better? The claim replaces “see” as its consequence.
rows.anchor: وقال سيبويه: أم هذه المعادلة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari likewise connects أم to the preceding question, with “I am better” standing for the seeing that would lead them to say so.
rows.anchor: وهذا من إنزال السبب منزلة المسبب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan calls the connected analysis strained: an alternative must parallel the prior clause, and “I am better” cannot be reconstructed as a matching clause to “Do you not see?”
rows.anchor: وهذا القول متكلف جدا، إذ المعادل إنما يكون مقابلا للسابق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A verb phrase generally pairs with a verb phrase, while a noun phrase pairs with a noun phrase or a clause reconstructible as one; the cited examples illustrate the rule.
rows.anchor: وإن كان السابق اسما، كان المعادل اسما، أو جملة فعلية يتقدر منها اسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deleting the comparison after أم is allowed when لا remains, but deleting it without لا is not normal usage.
rows.anchor: فأما حذفه دون لا، فليس من كلامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Omitting أم and its counterpart is rare; the poet's line that follows is offered as an example.
rows.anchor: وقد جاء حذف أم والمعادل، وهو قليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison poem uses أم as a transition, illustrating the reading of بل.
rows.anchor: بدت مثل قرن الشمس في رونق الضحى ... وصورتها أم أنت في العين أملح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poet's example of dropping أم and its counterpart means “or error” after saying he does not know whether the suitor seeks guidance.
rows.anchor: يريد أم غي

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority says Moses' speech still bore a trace of the ember he had swallowed.
rows.anchor: الجمهور، أنه كان بلسانه بعض شيء من أثر الجمرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who say God answered Moses' prayer about his speech explain “he scarcely makes himself clear” as inability to state his proof convincingly.
rows.anchor: جعل انتفاء الإبانة بأنه لا يبين حجته الدالة على صدقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says Pharaoh mocked Moses' low status from his years in Pharaoh's household and exaggerated what he remembered.
rows.anchor: فنسب إلى ما عهده مبالغة في التعبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan calls Pharaoh's claim a sheer lie: Moses debated him, answered him, and defeated him with proof; all prophets are eloquent.
rows.anchor: وقول فرعون: ولا يكاد يبين، كذب بحت

rows.speaker: الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Baqir reads يبين with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, from بان meaning “to appear.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الباقر: يبين، بفتح الياء، من بان إذا ظهر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says people who were appointed rulers wore two gold bracelets and a gold collar as signs of their authority.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: كانوا إذا سودوا رجلا، سوروه سوارين وطوقوه بطوق من ذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh argues that if Moses were truthful, his Lord would have invested him with royal authority, contrasting this with Moses' weakness and few supporters.
rows.anchor: وكان ذلك دليلا على إلقاء مقاليد الملك إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's taunt also implies that a truthful Moses should have been made king and supported by angels.
rows.anchor: إن كان صادقا، فهلا ملكه ربه وسوره وجعل الملائكة أنصاره

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak reads the verb actively: “Why did God not cast bracelets of gold upon him?”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الضحاك: فلولا ألقي مبنيا للفاعل

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority reads the verb passively, with أساورة in the nominative.
rows.anchor: والجمهور: أساورة رفعا

rows.speaker: أبي وعبد الله
rows.claim: Ubayy and Abdullah read أساوير; its singular is إسوار, equivalent to سوار, with the ending replacing a yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وأبي وعبد الله: أساوير، والمفرد إسوار بمعنى سوار

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan, Qatada, Abu Raja, al-Araj, Mujahid, Abu Haywa, and Hafs read أسورة as the plural of سوار, on the pattern of خمار and أخمرة.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن، وقتادة، وأبو رجاء، والأعرج، ومجاهد، وأبو حيوة، وحفص: أسورة

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-A'mash reads أساور, also reported from Ubayy and Abu Amr.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش: أساور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels accompanying Moses would protect him and establish his argument.
rows.anchor: أي يحمونه ويقيمون حجته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the angels would help Moses against those who opposed him.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يعينونه على من خالفه

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says the angels would accompany one another.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: يقارن بعضهم بعضا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the angels would walk with Moses.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: يمشون معه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the angels would follow one another in succession.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: متتابعين

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-A'rabi says Pharaoh made his people seem foolish because their understanding was light.
rows.anchor: أي استجهلهم لخفة أحلامهم، قاله ابن الأعرابي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says Pharaoh made them pliant and easily led, and their wickedness made them obey him.
rows.anchor: حملهم على أن يخفوا لما يريد منهم، فأجابوه لفسقهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb in “when they angered Us” is causative; Pharaoh's people committed vile deeds that meant God would no longer forbear with them.
rows.anchor: فلما عملوا الأعمال الخبيثة الموجبة لأن لا يحلم عنهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says they grieved God's believing allies, including the magicians and the Children of Israel.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: أحزنوا أولياءنا المؤمنين نحو السحرة وبني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A second report from Ibn Abbas says the people angered God.
rows.anchor: وعنه أيضا: أغضبونا

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali says the people provoked God's displeasure.
rows.anchor: وعن علي: أسخطونا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation takes the phrase to mean that they opposed God.
rows.anchor: وقيل: خالفوا

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri and others distinguish God's anger as the will to punish, an attribute of essence, from punishment itself, an attribute of action.
rows.anchor: وقال القشيري وغيره: الغضب من الله، أما إرادة العقوبة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority reads سلفا with fatḥa on both consonants.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: سلفا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Zayd ibn Aslam, and Qatada interpret سلفا as people who went ahead to the Fire.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس، وزيد بن أسلم، وقتادة: أي متقدمين إلى النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root means to go ahead; salaf can also mean earlier forefathers, with the plurals أسلاف and سلاف.
rows.anchor: وهو مصدر سلف يسلف سلفا، وسلف الرجل آباؤه المتقدمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis makes سلفا a plural of سالف, like حارس and حرس, though Abu Hayyan says it is really a collective noun.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو جمع سالف، كحارس وحرس

rows.speaker: طفيل
rows.claim: Tufayl's elegy describes the dead as having gone ahead along the path, illustrating the sense of those who preceded.
rows.anchor: وقال طفيل يرثي قومه: مضوا سلفا قصد السبيل عليهم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra and al-Zajjaj say Pharaoh's people became a precedent from which the Prophet's contemporaries could learn.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء والزجاج: سلفا ليتعظ بهم الكفار المعاصرون للرسول

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله وأصحابه
rows.claim: Abu Abdullah and his companions, Sa'id ibn Iyad, al-A'mash, Talha, al-Araj, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read سلفا with both consonants rounded, as the plural of سليف, a group.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عبد الله وأصحابه، وسعيد بن عياض، والأعمش، وطلحة، والأعرج، وحمزة، والكسائي

rows.speaker: القاسم بن معن
rows.claim: Al-Qasim ibn Ma'n heard Arabs say مضى سليف من الناس, confirming the meaning “a group of people.”
rows.anchor: سمع القاسم بن معن العرب تقول: مضى سليف من الناس

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali, Mujahid, and al-Araj also read the word with both vowels rounded, as the plural of سلفة, meaning a community or group.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علي، ومجاهد، والأعرج أيضا: وسلفا، بضم السين واللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In another usage, السلف means an ugly or shameful child, plural سلفان.
rows.anchor: والسلف في غير هذا: ولد القبح، والجمع سلفان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “An example for later peoples” means a remarkable story that circulated like a proverb: later disbelievers would be told they resembled Pharaoh's people.
rows.anchor: أي حديثا عجيب الشأن سائرا مسير المثل
